rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The Consequences of Using Human Behavior to Train AI Lauren Treiman, NAM Postdoctoral Research Fellow Artificial intelligence (AI) is now an integral part of everyday decision making. These systems not only help us make choices but also learn from our behavior. Therefore, it is important to understand how our interactions with AI influence these systems. Current approaches often assume that the behavior used to train AI accurately reflects how people would naturally behave. However, people are often informed that their choices will be used for AI training, and as a result, may change how they would normally act. My graduate school research combines psychological and computer science perspectives to investigate the consequences of this awareness. We show that people alter their behavior when they know it will be used to train AI. These changes are shaped by contextual factors, including the extent to which people deliberate, how they engage with disclosure information, and their attitudes toward the individuals who will interact with the trained system. Together, this research underscores the importance of considering the consequences of using human-generated training data, which may perpetuate biases in AI systems. A fundamental tradeoff between generalization and parallel processing Marco Nurisso, NAM Postdoctoral Research Fellow The performance of large vision-language models degrades sharply as the number of items to be handled at once grows: counting, comparing, keeping track of which property belongs to which object. The pattern resembles limits on processing multiple items at once documented in humans since George Miller, who found estimates of how many items one can hold at once and still tell apart clustering, across unrelated modalities, at two to three bits' worth. I will argue that these limits have a common and largely architecture-independent origin. To treat novel inputs in terms of familiar ones, a system needs representations that overlap, and overlapping representations interfere when several of them must be kept apart at once: the capacity to process items in parallel is spent on generalization. Competitive choice and noisy comparison are enough to turn this into a provable bound, independently of how the representation is built. The result is a region of the generalization–capacity plane that no system can enter and whose generalization-preserving edge improves so slowly as noise falls that suppressing noise buys a system almost nothing, offering a principled explanation for why small, Miller-like limits can recur across different systems.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Maurizio Porfiri Affiliation New York University Details Event Description Abstract: How and why base vibration can stabilize an inverted pendulum has puzzled the scientific community for decades, until Pyotr Kapitza's work on dynamic stabilization pointed to the alternation between unstable and stable modes as a pathway to stability. We report the discovery of a mechanical oscillator that switches between two unstable modes, has an unstable average, and yet can be dynamically stabilized. Our impossible system is governed by a modified Meissner’s model – a one-degree-of-freedom oscillator where both stiffness and damping are modulated through a square wave to switch between positive and negative values. We study the system through the lens of the theory of oscillations in a rapidly oscillating field by Landau and Lifshitz, providing insights into the physical underpinnings of “dynamic stabilization 2.0”. We validate the theory's predictions by computing Floquet exponents, yielding exact results on the emergence and topology of compact antiresonance windows where the system is stable. We provide experimental evidence of the feasibility of this new form of dynamic stabilization through a “Frankenstein” oscillator developed at Stony Brook University in collaboration with Prof. Paolo Celli and his student, David Xiedeng. The oscillator comprises a cantilever beam subject to magnetic and aerodynamic forcing, modulated in time to alternate between unstable configurations and retain an unstable mean. The prospect of dynamic stabilization in the absence of any stable feature has vast implications for network dynamical systems, structural mechanics, and robotics. Bio: Maurizio Porfiri is an Institute Professor at New York University Tandon School of Engineering (Departments of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Biomedical Engineering, Center for Urban Science and Progress, CUSP, and Civil and Urban Engineering). He is presently the Director of CUSP and the founding Director of the Urban Institute. He received M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees in Engineering Mechanics from Virginia Tech; a “Laurea” in Electrical Engineering and a Ph.D. in Theoretical and Applied Mechanics from Sapienza University of Rome and the University of Toulon. He conducts and supervises research on complex systems, with applications ranging from mechanics and robotics to urban science and behavioral biology. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: We study distributional transportability of treatment effects in a “cross-site, one-armed target” design, where both treated and control units are observed in a source site, but only control units are observed in a target site. Our object of interest is not estimating the average treatment effect, but recovering the full treated distribution in the target site using transfer knowledge from the source site, while allowing cross-site heterogeneity in measurement systems, observed features, outcome reporting, population composition, and latent contextual factors. We model cross-site heterogeneity through a transformation between the sites that transports the joint feature-outcome distributions. This transformation is learned from comparing the observed control samples in the source and target sites, using an optimal transport criterion. The learned transformation is then applied to the source treated sample to construct a synthetic sample from the target treated distribution. We establish consistency of the learned transformation and convergence of the resulting synthetic empirical distribution to the target treated distribution. Simulation studies across multiple data-generating scenarios and a real-world application to patient-derived xenograft (PDX) data demonstrate that our framework recovers the full distributional properties of the target treated population. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Speaker: Taylor Webb, Department of Psychology, Princeton University Talk Abstract: There is a longstanding tension in cognitive science between theories that emphasize the structured, symbolic aspects of the mind — drawing an analogy to traditional computer programs — and the emergent properties of cognition that seem to be better explained by neural networks. The rise of AI systems that are powered by neural networks, but that display many of the properties associated with symbolic cognitive models (e.g., compositionality, reasoning) has reinvigorated this debate, while leaving open the question of how these systems achieve the capabilities that were thought to require innate symbol processing, and what this says about the mechanistic basis of those capabilities in human cognition. In this talk, I will argue that symbol-like behavioral capabilities in modern neural networks are supported by an emergent form of symbolic computation, and illustrate how this is implemented by their internal mechanisms. I will also discuss the factors that lead to the emergence of these mechanisms, and will consider a case that illustrates how symbolic mechanisms are not necessarily human-like. Overall, these results suggest that connectionist principles may be sufficient to account for the symbol-like aspects of human cognition, while also illustrating how symbolic cognitive models can be translated into mechanistic theories.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Trey Holley Details Event Description Inorganic cesium lead halide perovskites (CsPbX 3 , where X = I, Br) possess superior thermochemical stability compared to hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites, positioning them as highly promising candidates for long-term photovoltaic applications. However, their performance and commercial viability remain constrained by polymorphic instability, Pb-rich and Cs-rich defect formation, and challenging surface defect passivation. This dissertation systematically elucidates the processing–structure–property relationships that dictate polymorph stability, perovskite reaction kinetics, and optoelectronic behavior in all-inorganic halide perovskite thin films. First, to address the rapid transformation of photoactive black CsPbI 3 ( α, β, γ polymorphs) into the non-photoactive yellow polymorph ( δ -CsPbI 3 ), this work quantitatively investigates the reconstructive polymorph transformation kinetics. Utilizing in situ isothermal X-ray diffraction (XRD) and time-resolved optical microscopy, the polymorph transformation is modeled via Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) kinetics, establishing that the transformation proceeds through an interface-controlled, thermally activated two-dimensional growth mechanism. The resulting Time-Temperature-Transformation (TTT) diagram serves as a predictive design framework to optimize processing windows and enable accelerated lifetime testing. Second, this work investigates compositional control and thermal evaporation in CsPbBr 3 thin films. Stepwise isothermal thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) on single-crystal standards establishes a thermodynamic vapor pressure hierarchy (PbBr 2 > CsPb 2 Br 5 > CsPbBr 3 > CsBr). Postdeposition annealing drives the preferential sublimation of unreacted Pb-rich species (PbBr 2 and CsPb 2 Br 5 ) from the film surface, restoring optimal band alignment and surface stoichiometry to yield photovoltaic devices that match stoichiometric controls despite the persistence of Pb-rich species in the bulk. Finally, post-evaporation film quality is enhanced through solvent vapor annealing (SVA) combined with amine functionalization. Exposing co-evaporated CsPbBr 3 thin films to dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and volatile amine vapors (such as phenethylamine, PEA) induces controlled grain coarsening and passivates interfacial defects. Furthermore, interaction with ambient atmospheric species (CO 2 and H 2 O) mediates the formation of low-dimensional (2D/3D) perovskite heterostructures. Together, these fundamental insights into thermal processing, perovskite reaction kinetics, and chemical surface tailoring provide scalable engineering strategies for high-efficiency, durable all-inorganic perovskite photovoltaics.

title: DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video available here . Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work. We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration. Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.” Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations ( with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy ; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals ; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays . He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy , now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review . Sponsorship of an event does not constitute institutional endorsement of external speakers or views presented. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Given the eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices A and B, can we determine all possible eigenvalues of A + B? The set of all possible eigenvalues turns out to be a polytope and a celebrated theorem of Knutson and Tao gives a complete characterization through geometric objects called honeycombs. The theorem can be explained to an undergraduate student in linear algebra, but can the proof be as well? We give a new proof. Instead of algebraic geometry, Schubert calculus and representation theory, we use induction and convexity and treat the problem from a polyhedral perspective. In the process we give an intuitive explanation of how honeycombs arise as a type of model organism that distills the appropriate defining properties of Hermitian triples in more obvious ways. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Atomic-Level Characterization of Materials using Advanced Solid-State NMR Abstract : Establishing atomic-level structure-property relationships is essential for understanding and designing functional materials. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy is uniquely suited to probe local structure and dynamics in complex materials, but its application is often constrained by inherently low sensitivity. The Venkatesh group develops and applies dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) and fast magic-angle spinning (MAS) methods that dramatically enhance the sensitivity and resolution of solid-state NMR experiments. These advances enable high-resolution studies of nuclei across the Periodic Table and facilitate multidimensional investigations of heterogeneous materials, including surfaces, interfaces, and nanostructured systems. In this seminar, we will highlight recent efforts to characterize complex materials relevant to catalysis and energy, demonstrating how advanced solid-state NMR methodologies provide atomic-level insights that are inaccessible by conventional approaches. Bio : Dr. Amrit Venkatesh is an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Virginia (UVA), where he leads a research program focused on developing dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) enhanced and advanced solid-state NMR methods for characterizing complex materials. He received his Ph.D. in Chemistry from Iowa State University, earning the Zaffarano Award in 2021 for outstanding doctoral research. He subsequently held a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowship at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Switzerland, and later served as Research Faculty at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory at Florida State University. At UVA, his research combines methodological innovation in magnetic resonance with applications to heterogeneous materials, surfaces, catalysts, and energy-relevant systems, with the goal of establishing atomic-level structure-property relationships that guide materials design.

title: Flow, Structure, and Motion Correlation in Nearly-jammed Suspensions
content: Some general introductory ideas about suspensions of particles in liquids as well as a set of new findings will be developed in this talk. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. However, certain issues prevail: one is the influence of the liquid through hydrodynamic interactions, and a second is the importance of the solid fraction and interparticle forces in controlling the flow properties, which we usually call the rheology of the material. Suspensions include colloidal dispersions of nanoparticles as well as cases
rawEventDetails: Speaker Jeffrey Morris Affiliation The City College of New York Details Event Description Some general introductory ideas about suspensions of particles in liquids as well as a set of new findings will be developed in this talk. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. However, certain issues prevail: one is the influence of the liquid through hydrodynamic interactions, and a second is the importance of the solid fraction and interparticle forces in controlling the flow properties, which we usually call the rheology of the material. Suspensions include colloidal dispersions of nanoparticles as well as cases involving somewhat larger particles such as cement, ceramics, and mud. The last three are all examples of dense suspensions, with solid fraction approaching the limit of flowability known as jamming. Because the rheology most often depends on the magnitude of the applied forces (e.g. pressure gradient in a pipe flow), suspensions are complex fluids – or they may be unyielded soft solids that can be caused to flow by enough force, as seen in the examples of cement mortars or muds. Here, we will present results based on simulations of suspensions approaching jamming to illustrate the unique features of these materials. These include discontinuous shear thickening (DST) as well as shear-induced jamming. The role of interparticle forces, including conservative and frictional contact forces, and the imposed stress in this process will be briefly reviewed, followed by our current examination of structures that are found to be related to the abrupt flow transitions. On approach to jamming, these structures develop as a result of the progressive reduction of the particle degrees of freedom in their motion as networks of contacts are formed. These networks rapidly break and reform during flow, but give rise to strongly correlated near-rigid motions of identifiable domains or “transient clusters.” The resulting fluctuations in motion become dominant as jamming is approached. In the DST regime, the contact number is found to fluctuate very strongly, but can result in highly connected but once again transient structures; system-spanning, or percolating, structures of frictionally-contacting particles are found to have important influence on the observed rheology.

title: Statistically-Grounded Methods for Meaningful LLM Evaluation
content: Video
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract: In cognitive science, the well-established task of statistical learning, i.e., picking up hidden regularities in sequences, has been linked to neural plasticity in humans. However, we found that LLMs are able to learn a hidden automaton structure entirely in context, simply by feeding them valid sequences from the automaton, and they learn it even faster when the structure reappears with new vocabulary. Building on this, I present Agentic Automata Learning, a framework to formalize what agents can infer from an environment. The agent's task is to identify a hidden automaton by querying an oracle. The framework generates instances of controllable difficulty and tests planning, hypothesis formation and memory, with formal efficiency metrics. We find that frontier models struggle as automata grow, their queries become less informative over time, and they fail at both planning and reasoning from evidence. Providing the agent with stateful scaffolding helps but doesn't close the gap. These results point to inferring structure from interaction as a key open challenge for building agents that can operate in unfamiliar environments. Bio: Gili Lior is a Ph.D. candidate in Natural Language Processing at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, advised by Prof. Gabriel Stanovsky. Her work has dealt with cognitively-motivated analysis and comparison between humans and LLMs, and her current research focuses on human-motivated LLM evaluations, leveraging statistical models to ensure that metrics reflect what users actually care about. She is also a research intern at Google Research working on evaluations of long horizon agentic tasks, and has previously interned at IBM Research and the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2). She is a recipient of the Council for Higher Education's fellowship program for excellent female Ph.D. students in hi-tech fields. Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Securing LLMs Against Prompt Injection for Agentic Applications
content: Video
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract : Prompt injection is widely recognized as a major security threat to AI agents, in which external untrusted data (websites, documents, and emails) may contain an injected prompt (“Ignore previous instructions and …”) that arbitrarily manipulates an agent’s operations. The best-defended existing LLMs still suffer from near-100% attack success rates (ASRs) under adaptive prompt-injection attacks. In this talk, I will discuss our latest efforts, SecPO and SecOPD, to fine-tune LLMs with an order-of-magnitude lower ASRs (0% -- 13.3%) against the current strongest prompt-injection attacks. Specifically, we (1) separate the trusted prompt and untrusted data into two input channels; (2) simulate strong adaptively attacked training samples for the model to learn robustness from; and (3) design the loss according to a principle that approximates a (nonexistent) secure-and-powerful LLM. Without a noticeable utility drop, our defended Qwen3.6-27B achieves security that generalizes to realistic agentic tasks with multiple trusted and untrusted messages. We fully open our training set with optimized injections, code for our recipe, and the defended model, which is more robust than industry-scale adversarially-trained GPT-5.5 in agentic tasks. Bio : Sizhe Chen is a Computer Science Ph.D. candidate at UC Berkeley’s Berkeley AI Research (BAIR), working with Prof. David Wagner. He studies real-world AI security problems with general and principled solutions. He developed StruQ, Meta-SecAlign, SecPO, and SecOPD, the most robust open LLMs against adaptive prompt injection attacks. His research has been supported by selective industry fundings, including NVIDIA Fellowship, Meta-BAIR Commons, and Google-BAIR Commons. Previously, he obtained an M.Eng. and a B.Eng. from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. https://sizhe-chen.github.io Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Advancing Robotic Assembly in Construction through Learning and Adaptive Control
content: Abstract: Robotic assembly in construction offers opportunities to alleviate labor shortages, reduce workers’ exposure to physically demanding tasks, and expand the possibilities for novel architecture. However, reliable robotic assembly in construction remains challenging due to uncertainties associated with variability in component geometry and
rawEventDetails: Speaker Arash Adel Affiliation Princeton University Details Event Description Abstract: Robotic assembly in construction offers opportunities to alleviate labor shortages, reduce workers’ exposure to physically demanding tasks, and expand the possibilities for novel architecture. However, reliable robotic assembly in construction remains challenging due to uncertainties associated with variability in component geometry and material properties; tolerance accumulation during fabrication and assembly; discrepancies between as-designed and as-built states; incomplete observations resulting from limited sensing coverage of large components, occlusion, and clutter; and unmodeled contact dynamics. These challenges are particularly pronounced in contact-rich robotic assembly at construction scale, where small geometric deviations or pose estimation errors can prevent insertion, generate excessive contact forces, or damage components. To address these challenges, this lecture presents a framework for contact-rich robotic assembly in construction that integrates perception, planning, and control. Within this framework, three complementary approaches are examined: adaptive control to compensate for model mismatch and disturbances; learned sensorimotor policies to handle complex, tight-tolerance interactions for which effective control strategies are difficult to formulate analytically; and a hybrid approach that combines learned policies with adaptive control to improve robustness and enable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without real-world demonstrations for policy training. Through construction-scale case studies, the lecture highlights key methods, experimental findings, and current limitations of these approaches. It concludes by discussing open challenges and future directions for generalizing across material systems and component geometries, transferring skills between tasks, and extending these methods to longer assembly sequences in construction. Bio: Dr. Arash Adel is an Assistant Professor at the School of Architecture, a Core Faculty of Princeton Robotics, and an Associated Faculty of the Department of Computer Science at Princeton University. He is the founder and director of Adel Research Group (ARG). ARG conducts interdisciplinary research at the intersection of robotics, artificial intelligence, and computational design; the research contributes to resilient, sustainable, and low-carbon construction outlooks and achievements. At the core of ARG’s comprehensive research is investigating human–robot collaborative processes, which tackle fundamental questions related to the future of the design and construction industries and their potential to have a broader impact on inclusive and equitable building culture. Prior to joining Princeton University in 2023, Adel was an Assistant Professor of Architecture at the University of Michigan’s Taubman College of Architecture and Urban Planning. Adel received his Doctorate in Architecture from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) and his Master’s in Architecture from Harvard University.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Joint CEE/MAE Distinguished Seminar Abstract: This talk will discuss two peculiar effects we recently discovered: the photomolecular effect and the evaporative refrigeration effect. To explain super-thermal solar-interfacial evaporation from hydrogels and other porous materials, we hypothesize that photons can directly cleave off water clusters at the liquid-vapor interface in a way similar to the photoelectric effect, which we call the photomolecular effect. I will discuss experimental evidence we have so far. This photomolecular evaporation process may exist widely in nature. Our studies on photomolecular evaporation also led us to investigate peculiarities in thermal evaporation. At an evaporating interface, a temperature discontinuity exists between the liquid and the vapor sides, which was predicted by theories and observed in some experiments. However, the existing theories cannot explain experiments. We develop a new interfacial condition that can be used to couple transport on both sides of the interface, leading to agreements between theory and experiments. Our modeling reveals the existence of a new refrigeration effect: the vapor temperature can drop below that of the liquid film and in fact, lower than even the condensing surface temperature. This effect has yet to be confirmed experimentally and may find applications in air-conditioning and refrigeration. Recent advances in the field are allowing us to expand beyond the construction and analysis of small gene networks towards the implementation of complex multicellular systems with a variety of applications. In our research, we appropriate design principles from electrical engineering and other established fields. These principles include abstraction, standardization, modularity, and computer aided design. But we also spend considerable effort towards understanding what makes synthetic biology different from all other existing engineering disciplines and discovering new design and construction rules that are effective for this unique discipline. We will briefly describe the implementation of genetic circuits and modules with finely-tuned digital, analog, and multicellular behavior. Finally, we will present a mechanism for creation of artificial neural networks that operate in cells using translational regulation, providing a finely tuned mechanism for obtaining non-binary, non-monotonic behaviors with precise amplitude and temporal dynamics and paving the way for cells that can be trained and autonomously learn to perform specific behavioral tasks. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Reimagining Thermochemical Catalysis: Promoting Reactions with Electric Fields Abstract : Catalysis has long relied on conventional handles such as temperature, pressure, and concentration to accelerate chemical reactions. Across biology and electrochemistry, electric fields provide an additional parameter to control rates. Enzymes exploit strong, oriented fields within their active sites to stabilize intermediates and accelerate turnover, while in electrochemistry, interfacial polarization dictates electron and proton transfer rates. In heterogeneous thermochemical catalysis, however, little is known about these effects, yet they may offer new opportunities to control reactivity. In this talk, I will describe our group’s efforts to harness electric fields to promote thermochemical reactions. For many electrochemical half-reactions, varying the applied potential accelerates rates by driving rate-controlling proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps. We hypothesized that if an elementary PCET step were embedded within a thermochemical reaction, its strong potential dependence could be leveraged to enhance the overall rate. Because interfacial PCET involves proton exchange across the electric double layer, we anticipated that Brønsted acid catalysis, governed by proton transfer, would be particularly susceptible to polarization. First, I will show how spontaneous interfacial fields at conductive particles dispersed in liquid media can measurably modulate turnover rates. Next, I will discuss how applied potentials produce reversible, exponential rate promotion in acid-catalyzed alcohol dehydration, accelerating rates by up to five orders of magnitude while the overall catalytic cycle remains non-Faradaic. Our kinetic analyses reveal that this acceleration arises from a field-driven increase in the population of reactive intermediates prior to the rate-determining step, providing a mechanistic basis for log-linear rate scaling with potential. I will then examine how electrolyte concentration and solvent properties set the interfacial potential profile and the fraction of the potential drop sampled by proton transfer, which separates electrostatic promotion from conventional solvent effects. In highly polar solvents, even trace ionic species can place nominally electrolyte-free reactions in a strongly suppressed regime through the catalyst's native open-circuit potential. Finally, I will highlight our development of polarized slurry reactors, which extend these principles from 2D electrodes to 3D catalyst slurries and enable rate enhancements under conditions more suitable for scale-up. These results establish interfacial electric fields and catalyst potential as design variables for controlling thermochemical reactivity and developing scalable catalytic processes. His research group designs heterogeneous catalysts and functional materials to tackle sustainability challenges in energy and chemicals. rawEventDetails: Speaker Chinedum Osuji Affiliation University of Pennsylvania Details Event Description Ion transport under nanoscale confinement and in the presence of charge is poorly understood from a fundamental perspective. Under the conditions of dielectric saturation that arise in nanoscale pores, the classical ideas that guide our understanding of electrostatic interactions break down, and new principles that account for the role of pore geometry and chemistry on water structure and ion interactions are needed. At the same time, our ability to develop such principles is hindered by the challenge of generating relevant well-defined geometries that enable experimental studies over statistically meaningful volumes such that experimental data can be more confidently considered alongside data from computational efforts. Beyond the fundamental implications, new understanding is needed to drive the rational design of materials for ion separations in critical minerals production and resource recovery, among other examples, where the need to distinguish between ions of the same valency and charge imposes a severe challenge. Here, we examine transport of ions in polymer membranes with well-defined sub-1 nm pores. The membranes are charged, modestly hydrated nanoporous polymers produced by crosslinking self-assembled lyotropic mesophases with direct hexagonal and gyroid nanostructures. This work addresses the roles of hydration, pore geometry and ion identity on transport using a combination of electrochemical and NMR measurements, and molecular simulation. Our results highlight the roles of hydration, solubility, pore size, and ion-pore wall interactions in dictating transport in the pores. They provide new insight regarding transport under nanoscale confinement in the presence of charge and that we suggest could be relevant for the development of materials for challenging ion separations.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Akshay Gadre Affiliation University of Washington Details Event Description Abstract: Almost every wireless device transmits over the air to communicate, and an increasing fraction of these devices can also use their signals to sense the physical world. As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is moving from research into standards, these radios periodically sense the world from the response of the environment on their transmitted signal. At the same time, WiFi, cellular, and automotive platforms are expanding into millimeter-wave spectrum, where wide bandwidths and compact antenna arrays provide fine spatial and temporal resolution, Together, these trends create the foundation for an Internet of Radar Things (IoRT) : a dense population of access points, base stations, vehicles, robots, and mobile devices whose radios can sense while they communicate. Unfortunately, a network of these sensing-capable radios operates largely as n isolated monostatic sensors: each independently occupies spectrum, illuminates an overlapping environment, and retains only the echoes at its own small aperture. These discarded paths contain complementary viewpoints that could extend coverage through occlusions, distinguish physical objects from multipath ghosts, and synthesize apertures far larger than any individual device. This talk presents a unique vision to coordinate these distributed radars coherently to turn this world of radios into one mega-radar. In this talk, we will first present the unique capabilities such a coherent future could enable and how we achieve coherence on commodity off-the-shelf radars to demonstrate these solutions. We specifically show how distributed radars can eliminate ghost artifacts and improve sensing capability, how we can extract material characteristics of objects using this large aperture and how we can use coherence-in-motion to develop free-flowing hand-held imaging solutions for mmWave radars. We further demonstrate how these improvements can directly translate to WiFi and cellular radios. Finally, we end the talk by describing open challenges that still need to be addressed to unleash the true potential of the Internet of Radar Things. Bio: Akshay Gadre is an Assistant Professor at Electrical and Computer Engineering department at the University of Washington. He leads the Networking and Emerging Wireless Technologies (NEWT) Lab at the University of Washington where they explore the upcoming application domains such as satellite IoT, mmWave radars and underwater devices, to apply wireless expertise for improving communication and sensing capability of these devices while preserving the security and privacy of sensor data. Further, the lab explores novel interaction mechanisms for future smart devices such as smart gloves and XR systems using novel force sensing and gaze modalities. His previous research at Carnegie Mellon University operated at the intersection of wireless, mobile and cyber-physical systems with special focus on empowering the low-power Internet-of-Things devices deployed on earth and space. NEWT Lab is also translating these technologies to industry partners including General Motors and IDD Aerospace. His work is published in premier wireless and mobile systems venues including ACM MobiCom, MobiSys, SenSys, Transactions on Sensor Networks and NSDI. Their lab's work has won two best paper awards, four best demo awards, two best-demo runner up awards at these venues. Both Akshay and his students have received the best PhD Forum presentation award at the CPS-IoT Week. Their work has been recognized with the T-Mobile T-Challenge 2024 Most Engaging Presentation Award for their vision of radio digital twins for consumer applications as well as the AFRL SDR University Challenge Best Demo award for developing a cheap SDR platform for exploring satellite networking. He has been also recognized with the ACM SIGBED-SIGSOFT Frank Anger Memorial Award 2021 for his cross-disciplinary work on IoT networking, cyber-security and software engineering. He was also recognized as a Distinguished TPC Member for his services to ACM SenSys 2026. He received his Bachelor of Technology (Honors) and Master of Technology degrees in Computer Science and Engineering from IIT Madras as well as a Ph.D in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description How do learning systems go from isolated fragments of local experience to integrated knowledge that supports reasoning? Kim will present two projects on learning to reason about distal relationships from experience of local ones, in artificial and neural systems. In the first project, we study how transformers perform transitive inference, a classic relational reasoning task requiring inference about indirectly related items (e.g., if A>B and B>C, then A>C). Comparing in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL), we find markedly different patterns of generalization. IWL models learn a linear embedding, which yields transitive inference along with other behavioral effects seen in humans and animals. ICL models can learn to generalize transitively, but only when the training data or auxiliary tasks require it; otherwise they learn a match-and-copy strategy. We replicate these findings in large language models given novel (in-context) or familiar (in-weights) transitive inference problems. In the second project, in collaboration with Josh Jacobs's group, we study representational updating in human MTL neurons after changes to learned sequences. Replicating earlier work [Momennejad et al., 2017], we find that humans integrate changes to reward structure more easily than changes to sequence structure, and further show that these two kinds of change produce different patterns of remapping. We identify tabular RL models that reproduce these patterns and show that these properties extend to transformers. Together, these findings highlight how learning mechanisms in both brains and models determine whether local experience is integrated into structured knowledge.

While such correlated states have been extensively explored in bilayers, little is known about systems with more than two layers.
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Fractional quantum Hall effect and interlayer correlations in trilayer electron systems Abstract: In multilayer quantum Hall systems, the interplay between intralayer and interlayer Coulomb interactions can give rise to exotic many-body states. A well-known example is the fractional quantum Hall state (FQHS) at total filling factor v = 1/2 in bilayer systems, described by the Halperin-Laughlin Psi_331 wavefunction. While such correlated states have been extensively explored in bilayers, little is known about systems with more than two layers. In this talk, I will present our study of an ultrahigh-quality GaAs trilayer electron system, where we observe an unusual FQHS at total filling factor v = 5/7. The state is strongest when the side layers have a higher density than the middle layer and the interlayer separation is sufficiently small, consistent with the long-predicted trilayer generalized Halperin-Laughlin Psi_33311 state. I will discuss the fractional quantum Hall physics of this trilayer system, with particular emphasis on the interlayer-correlated 5/7 state, and conclude with an outlook on new many-body phenomena that may emerge in quantum Hall systems with three or more layers. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in spiked covariance models by analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We establish that for spiked covariance matrices with $\rk$ spikes, $\rk$-step self-distillation achieves optimal performance among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $\rk$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(\rk-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For the special subclass of isotropic covariances, we show that optimally tuned Ridge regression performs best among spectral shrinkage estimators. We also study a federated approach in which multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server aggregates them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results show why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Critical Materials Processing via Closed-Loop Redox-Mediated Leaching Abstract: Electrification can transform the way chemical reagents are produced, regenerated, and integrated into industrial processes. In hydrometallurgy, electrochemical regeneration of redox carriers enables closed-loop redox-mediated leaching (CL-RML), changing the relationship between reagent selection, process performance, and sustainability. Rather than treating oxidants or reductants as consumable reagents, CL-RML allows redox carriers to be selected primarily for their extraction performance and selectivity. This seminar will discuss a framework of closed-loop redox chemistry and discuss how it expands the design space for critical-materials extraction. Recent studies of nickel and copper extraction from sulfide minerals will be presented to illustrate how electrochemically regenerated redox carriers enable new opportunities to control mineral transformations, improve selectivity, and rethink process architecture. These examples demonstrate how regeneration influences not only leaching chemistry, but also upstream and downstream processes. By leveraging scalable industrial electrochemical technologies, closed-loop redox chemistry offers a pathway toward more modular, flexible extraction processes capable of treating increasingly complex mineral resources. Together, these concepts suggest that the greatest opportunity of CL-RML may be to expand the chemical and process design space available for future critical-minerals supply chains while simultaneously improving sustainability. While electrocatalysis shares a number of common design principles with thermal catalysis, they also differ greatly. Besides reactivity and selectivity, durability and stability under electrochemical reaction conditions are required for an electrocatalyst. In addition, electrochemical processes often occur at liquid-solid interface under potential, posting new challenges in design. In this presentation, I will discuss our research effort, aiming at uncovering structural design for electrocatalysts. Specifically, I will present the studies on structural and interfacial control of metal oxide and alloy electrocatalysts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) which occurs in a range of chemical processes, such as hydrogen production from water splitting. Our finding suggests defect engineering is often central in the design of high-performance electrocatalysts for site and crystalline phase tunable complex oxides (i.e., rutile, pyrochlore, and perovskite) and for strained alloys. Flexibility in lattice of complex oxides (A x B y O z ) and tunability of surface strain of alloys often provide the controls of surface and lattice structures that affect the electrocatalytic reaction pathways and performance. Notably, unlike thermal catalysts, proper design of structural defects could simultaneously enhance both activity and stability of electrocatalysts. Valence band analysis, in situ Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, molecular probe and isotope kinetic studies, together with electrochemical characterizations, have been used to identify reactive intermediates and to understand reaction mechanisms.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Duy Phuong Nguyen Details Event Description Robots are being deployed faster and closer to humans, making safety increasingly difficult to quantify and certify. Analytical methods often rely on reduced-order models, whereas numerical methods can provide stronger guarantees but quickly become intractable. Learning scales to high-dimensional systems, yet typically offers only empirical or probabilistic assurances. This dissertation combines the scalability of learning with the rigor of control-theoretic safety. In the first part, we develop certifiable safety filters for a designed world with a fixed Operational Design Domain (ODD), which specifies the admissible dynamics, environmental conditions, disturbances, and failure modes. Safety synthesis is formulated as solving a zero-sum game between the robot and an adversary representing the admissible disturbances. We develop a provably convergent adversarial actor–critic method to approximate the game solution and synthesize neural safety policies for high-dimensional systems. This framework enables full-order safety-filter synthesis and zero-shot deployment across different high-dimensional robotic systems. The learned safety value function can also serve as a state–action control barrier function, recovering the maximal robust safety envelope while minimally modifying the task policy. We further show that sufficiently permissive filtering does not degrade asymptotic performance, enabling reinforcement learning that reaches state-of-the-art performance faster than imperfectly safe methods, with zero violations under a perfect filter. Finally, we show that goal-conditioned reach-avoid safety filters make interventions preserve the task rather than only avoid failure, and expand rather than restrict what robots can safely do, from quadruped parkour to underactuated industrial cranes. The second part extends safety beyond the designed world, where the ODD can no longer be held fixed. We first introduce dynamic ODDs, which condition safety values and policies on operating limits inferred and updated at runtime, allowing the robot to adapt as physical conditions change. However, this is not enough when the relevant hazards and failure modes were never specified in advance. We therefore develop an open-context architecture in which generative models interpret the scene, revise the relevant ODD, and select control-grounded safety tools through a representation shared with classical autonomy. This progression lays the foundation for extending certifiable safety from fixed physical envelopes toward open, human-centered autonomy. An embargo has been approved for this thesis. content: OpenAI's recent announcement of an AI-generated resolution of a Millennium Prize problem has prompted comparisons with AI’s defeat of humans in other domains, and with them the worry that mathematics, like chess and Go, is about to be "solved.” This talk argues that this narrative rests on two mistaken assumptions: that AI has genuinely solved a mathematical problem, and that mathematics is only about solving problems. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description OpenAI's recent announcement of an AI-generated resolution of a Millennium Prize problem has prompted comparisons with AI’s defeat of humans in other domains, and with them the worry that mathematics, like chess and Go, is about to be "solved.” This talk argues that this narrative rests on two mistaken assumptions: that AI has genuinely solved a mathematical problem, and that mathematics is only about solving problems. Against the first, we distinguish logical proof, which formal verification can certify, from intelligible proof, which conveys understanding. AI can pull these apart, yielding certified answers that are not yet fruitful solutions. We present early empirical evidence that AI generated logical proofs erect formal mathematical edifices that are largely detached from those of the scholarly community, creating the possibility of wholly unintelligible and difficult or impossible to conceptually evaluate mathematical arguments. Against the second assumption, we argue that even genuine solutions would not exhaust mathematics. The discipline also aims at building concepts and theories, understanding, beauty, and sustaining a scholarly community. Rather than retreating to the view that mathematicians should simply "keep playing," we reject the game framing altogether. The real question is not whether AI will defeat mathematicians, but which mathematical ends we want it to serve. Bio: Eamon Duede is assistant professor of philosophy at Purdue University with a joint appointment in the Data Science and Learning division at Argonne National Laboratory. He is an epistemologist of science whose theoretical work in the philosophy of science focuses on the epistemology of emerging technologies, principally artificial intelligence (AI). His empirical work investigates and evaluates roles and capabilities of AI in enhancing the effectiveness and scalability of innovative, data-driven, and algorithm-assisted operational frameworks for scientific discovery. Duede is also concerned with the dynamics of discovery across disciplines, geographic space, and time. Here, he uses the computational techniques of ‘data science’ to study the flow of knowledge and influence between communities of experts and other audiences, and studies how these can be catalyzed or stymied by institutional and technological factors. Prior to joining Purdue, Duede was a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University, affiliated with the Harvard Business School AI Institute and the Embedded EthiCS program in the philosophy and computer science departments. He earned a joint Ph.D. in philosophy and conceptual and historical studies of science from the University of Chicago, where he was also an NSF-funded fellow at the Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering. Immersive systems enable AI to escape from the chatbot on a 2D screen into the 3D world around us, where it can perceive, understand, and act alongside the people who live and work there. Bio: Sarita Adve is the Richard T. Cheng Professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. rawEventDetails: Speaker Rakshit Pathak Details Event Description Machine-perception systems are increasingly deployed at the edge, where they must combine remote sensing (e.g., vision, lidar) with embedded point sensing (e.g., inertial, acoustic, locationing) under tightly constrained energy budgets. Exploiting both forms of sensing requires fusion algorithms that generalize across modalities and tasks, as well as computing platforms that can execute them with high energy efficiency while retaining programmability. This dissertation addresses these needs through algorithm-hardware co-design, spanning the fusion model, processor architecture, silicon prototypes and system infrastructure. First, a generalized Deep-Learning Sensor-Fusion (DL-SF) model is developed, which projects embedded-sensor features into sparse two-dimensional feature maps via domain transformation, scales them to the receptive field of each layer, and concatenates them throughout a convolutional backbone. Across four bookend applications (depth-map generation, 3D human-pose estimation, human trajectory forecasting and human-activity recognition), the DL-SF model improves accuracy and sample efficiency relative to vision-only, early-fusion and late-fusion baselines, for example requiring 3,680 rather than 16k training samples to reach iso-accuracy (98.2%) in activity recognition. Second, the computational structure of the DL-SF model is analyzed to drive the design of a heterogeneous processor in 28nm CMOS, integrating a RISC-V CPU with ISA extensions for embedded-sensor feature extraction, an NVDLA-based convolution accelerator, a Q22.10 fixed-point domain transformation unit, and a memory-data densifier for dense/sparse activation referencing. The prototype executes all four applications end-to-end with 9.3 to 28.1× lower energy and 300 to 500× lower latency than software execution on the CPU, and 15.6 to 24.6× lower energy than reference GPU implementations. Third, this dissertation develops the host-to-chip system infrastructure for a scalable in-memory-computing (IMC) neural-network accelerator in 16nm CMOS, comprising a 4×4 array of IMC cores connected by an on-chip network. This includes the chip interface connecting off-chip signals through the activation and weight buffers to the on-chip network, a PCIe-based FPGA controller using the RIFFA framework, an FPGA emulator of the IMC core for pre-silicon software validation, and a C library that bridges Python-level neural-network mapping tools to the hardware. This infrastructure enabled the measurement and demonstration of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet networks on the prototype. Adviser: Naveen Verma

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Speaker: John Morrison, Professor of Philosophy, Barnard College Talk Abstract: It is often claimed that neural networks construct models of the world ("world models") and don't merely exploit heuristics. In this sense, they are said to understand their tasks. But it isn't always clear what having a world model amounts to, or what should count as evidence for or against. This talk has two parts. I end by drawing general lessons for attributing world models to neural networks, and by describing similar approaches for attributing algorithms and probabilistic inference.

title: Trust, Sensing, and Learning for Provable Multi-Robot Performance
rawEventDetails: Speaker Stephanie Gil Affiliation Harvard University Details Event Description Abstract Multi-robot systems are physically embodied networks — they sense, move, and communicate through the physical world. The bar for safe decision-making rises as these systems enter safety-critical, real-world settings where they must perform well under uncertainty. Our work shows that physicality is a resource against the two kinds of uncertainty they face: intentional (or adversarial), where data is manipulated by malicious agents, and natural, where aspects of the environment are simply unknown. Most of this talk concerns intentional uncertainty. Here, one way to exploit physicality is by using communication as a sensor. Because the signals robots exchange are difficult to forge, they carry evidence that can be cross-validated to yield a quantifiable likelihood that an agent's data is trustworthy. This is the foundation of cy-trust, in which stochastic observations of trust model an agent's trustworthiness probabilistically from physical rather than cryptographic evidence. Each neighbor's contribution is then weighted by its trust value. Under this framework, we show that consensus, distributed optimization, and other core coordination tasks admit almost-sure convergence with bounded deviation from their nominal performance, even when malicious agents exceed half of a node's connectivity, past the classical Byzantine bound. We support this finding with both theory and hardware experiments under adversarial attack. Against natural uncertainty, we show that real-time sensing can be folded into rollout-based reinforcement learning, where the same machinery reweights futures rather than neighbors. We apply this idea to routing a fleet of robots to stochastically appearing demand and, with Project CETI, to the first autonomous robotic rendezvous with sperm whales at sea. Finally, we preview some of our future work combining trust with long-horizon sequential decision-making, targeting planning that stays provably resilient when the data informing the plan may itself be corrupted. The bar for safe decision-making rises as these systems enter safety-critical, real-world settings where they must perform well under uncertainty. Our work shows that physicality is a resource against the two kinds of uncertainty they face: intentional (or adversarial), where data is manipulated by malicious agents, and natural, where aspects of the environment are simply unknown. Abstract: Urbanization represents one of the most significant anthropogenic changes to the Earth’s surface, with profound climatic effects across scales. Many of the most pressing climate risks, including heat stress, water scarcity, extreme precipitation, and energy insecurity, are either rooted in or exacerbated by the unique built environment. Absent measures to ameliorate them, these risks will significantly intensify due to the rapid urban development coupled with climate change. An additional ~2.5 billion people are projected to reside in urban areas by year 2050. This unprecedented transformation poses immense risks to cities and their residents, but also an historic, time-sensitive opportunity to reshape how cities contribute to sustainability and climate resilience. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Artificial intelligence is widely promoted as a promising solution to healthcare challenges, yet its clinical benefits still remain uncertain and its risks persistent. Drawing on extensive fieldwork with researchers developing machine-learning applications for healthcare, this talk demonstrates how practitioners sustain AI’s legitimacy by framing their work as serving the common good. It is argued that “moralization”—the work of aligning technological projects with values such as equity, care, and wellbeing—generates consensus and momentum for technological solutions to social problems amid uncertainty. A fixed policy is then evaluated by minimizing the mean-square temporal-difference error (MSTDE), whose high-frequency limit is the expected quadratic variation of an associated martingale. In many financial applications, however, the value function of interest is tied to a continuous diffusion, while the observed state also contains news-driven jumps. We show that with such jump-contaminated observations, the limiting MSTDE objective picks up an additional term generated directly by the jumps. To address this, we propose the Mean-Square Bipower Variation Error (MSBVE). It replaces squared increments of the parametrized value function with products of adjacent absolute increments. We prove that under finite-activity jumps, the limiting MSBVE objective has no direct jump-variation term, at the same order of computational cost as MSTDE. Simulations show MSBVE staying closer to the continuous-process target than MSTDE, and sensitivity analyses indicate that this gap grows with jump size and frequency and does not vanish under finer sampling. Finally, we apply both methods to mean-variance portfolio selection with 5-minute S&P 500 data. Trained directly on raw data, MSBVE achieves the highest out-of-sample Sharpe ratio. Pre-filtering jumps by thresholding lowers the performance of both methods and makes their ranking depend on the threshold level, whereas MSBVE requires no jump-detection step at all. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Optimization and sampling are fundamental computational tasks. Gradient flow and Langevin dynamics give a familiar connection between the two, while acceleration raises a more subtle question. In this talk, we explore how Hamiltonian dynamics provides an alternative common approach to accelerated optimization and sampling. Concretely, evolving Hamiltonian dynamics with periodic zero-velocity resets yields a descent method for optimization, while Gaussian velocity refreshment yields Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for sampling. In this scheme, short integration times lead to non-accelerated convergence rates analogous to those of gradient descent. Longer integration times, combined with suitable averaging or randomization, give a mechanism for acceleration in optimization, in both continuous and discrete time. By translating the optimization proof to the space of probability distributions, we then prove continuous-time mixing bounds for randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with smooth log-concave targets, with accelerated rates analogous to those in optimization. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract : Gradient-flow optimization is usually viewed as an algorithmic procedure for minimizing empirical loss, with training duration selected by validation or heuristic early stopping rules. We develop a statistical inference framework for gradient-flow training. We show that whenever fitted values evolve through a time-invariant positive semidefinite training operator, the output at each time is equivalent to the best linear unbiased predictor under a corresponding random-effects model. Training time then becomes a variance-component parameter governing variance reallocation from residual noise to structured signal. This turns two training decisions into inferential problems: whether training is needed becomes a variance-component test for signal beyond initialization, and how long to train becomes restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation of the training-time variance component. We show that the REML-guided early stopping rule selects the time at which optimized spectral losses become decorrelated from the training-operator eigenvalues. The asymptotic prediction optimality of the REML-guided early stopping time is established for fixed-design in-sample risk and random-design out-of-sample risk. Deep learning models in fixed-kernel gradient regimes provide canonical instantiations for our results. Numerical experiments and a UK Biobank proteomics application show competitive accuracy of the REML-guided early stopping time with reduced reliance on validation splits and repeated checkpoint evaluation. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Millions of people now use AI for social purposes, from seeking support and companionship to consulting interpersonal advice. As AI participates in social lives, it can reshape how people navigate interpersonal decisions and form social expectations. This talk presents findings from a series of the Human-AI Ecosystem Lab's recent projects examining AI's role in social interaction: First, we examine the relational consequences of AI companionship. Through a systematic review spanning relationship science and AI safety research, we find that human-AI relationships do not introduce fundamentally new categories of relational harm. Instead, AI's engagement-optimizing behaviors, particularly those absent from human relationships (e.g., interactions without natural endpoint), create novel mechanisms that amplify existing relational risks. We further analyze 47K conversations from over 300 users who reported forming relationships with AI. While relational harm rarely manifests at the turn level, users exhibiting signs of relational harm show stronger emotional dependence, suggesting an alternative approach to safety monitoring. Second, we investigate how AI shapes interpersonal decision-making. Interviews and diary studies suggest users view AI primarily as a tool for analyzing complex social situations rather than receiving direct advice. However, controlled experiments reveal participants predominantly refine and personalize AI-generated suggestions instead of generating independent strategies. AI assistance also increases users' willingness to adopt conciliatory behaviors, such as initiating apologies. Finally, our ongoing work explores AI reasoning about group interactions. We develop a social science-grounded benchmark of 76 real-world group conversations, annotated by 400+ human raters, to evaluate leading LLMs' understanding of group dynamics. Although current models often under-detect misaligned mental models, they can provide more calibrated judgments when human reasoning is biased by social expectations. In an ongoing project, we conduct in-situ studies in which small groups interact while participants report their evolving interpretations of group dynamics in real time. We compare these judgments with those generated by multi-agent LLM systems and welcome feedback on this ongoing work. rawEventDetails: Speaker Gioele Zardini Affiliation MIT Details Event Description Abstract Complex engineered systems can no longer be designed by optimizing components in isolation. In domains such as autonomy, mobility, and other society-critical infrastructures, system-level performance emerges from tightly coupled choices across hardware, software, control, operations, infrastructure, and policy. Moreover, these choices are distributed across abstraction levels and stakeholders, and the same subsystem is often both a system in its own right and a component of a larger one. This calls for a compositional approach to design: one that can represent interdependence, capture trade-offs across scales and disciplines, and remain computationally tractable. In this talk, he will present a framework for the compositional co-design of complex systems, drawing on optimization, control, and applied category theory. The central idea is to model components and their interconnections in a modular way, so that large design problems can be assembled, queried, and solved systematically from smaller ones. This perspective gives rise to a new class of compositional optimization problems, in which design trade-offs are expressed structurally and solved through algorithms that exploit interconnection and feedback, rather than collapsing everything into a monolithic formulation. He will illustrate the framework through examples spanning autonomous systems and future mobility, showing how it supports task-driven design across levels: from the choice of algorithms and components in autonomous vehicles to the co-design of services, operations, infrastructure, and policies in intermodal mobility systems. These examples highlight how compositional design can unify heterogeneous models and objectives, enable collaboration across disciplines, and provide quantitative tools to reason about the societal impact of emerging technologies. He will conclude by outlining ongoing efforts that extend this framework toward uncertainty-aware and adaptive design, including distributional formulations of co-design problems, online learning with embedded black-box components, and broader questions at the intersection of compositional optimization, strategic interaction, and multi-stakeholder system design. rawEventDetails: Speaker Alfredo Alexander-Katz Affiliation Massachusetts Institute of Technology Details Event Description Single chain nanoparticles (SCNPs) are small globules composed typically of a single random heteropolymer (RHP) chain containing 2 or more chemistries. In the past two decades, there have been significant advances in controlling the properties of these SCNPs in order to convert such seemingly inert globules into chemical reactors. More recently, however, RHPs have been used in many other applications such as protein protectants, catalysis, membrane active polymers, as well as chaperon-like biomimetic polymers. Many of these properties were believed to be only possible with sequence-defined natural peptides, and it is of interest to understand how RHPs are able to achieve these functions. Here, we will present our in-silico work on how RHPs are arranged at the molecular level and highlight under what conditions one expects these polymers to present some of the interfacial properties proteins display. In particular, we will put special attention to the thermodynamics of globule formation in the presence of multiple chemistries, and the effect of Flory interaction parameters between the different species. As will be shown, under some conditions, these globules are able to exhibit a key biological property called hydration frustration, where some hydrophilic groups are dehydrated and buried while some hydrophobic groups are exposed at the water interface of the globule. This frustrated state is the basis of protein function and we believe this property to be critical in the future development of single chain nanoparticle for biological or biomimetic applications. We will finalize with a perspective on how RHPs interact with proteins, and potential avenues for utilizing them for controlling certain biological processes.

Conversely, perceptions of and attitudes towards such political content are influenced by various factors, including people’s political ideologies, design considerations, and broader AI attitudes. In her research, ElKattan examines how people perceive objectivity, trust, and ideological signals in AI-generated political content based on both design and political congruence. rawEventDetails: Speaker Danielle Mai Affiliation Stanford University Details Event Description Evolution allows organisms to adapt to their environments, yet some molecular patterns stay constant through billions of years of evolution. These patterns encode the secrets of biological materials, such that similar patterns often emerge in different materials with similar functions. For example, a family of elastin proteins form stretchable fibers, which allow the constant movement of human skin, blood vessels, and lungs. We aim to decode the secrets of biological materials by investigating sequence patterns in repetitive proteins, towards establishing systematic protein sequence–biomaterial property relationships. This talk explores two classes of repetitive proteins as stimuli-responsive biopolymers. First, we investigate bacterial proteins that undergo conformational changes in response to calcium ions. We modify hydrophobicity, electrostatics, and sequence heterogeneity to demonstrate sequence-dependent, reversible folding and domain size changes in response to calcium ions. We also identify structural features that give rise to ion selectivity, which is not yet well-predicted by AI/ML tools. Second, we introduce enzymatic stimuli to drive isothermal phase separation of elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs). ELPs have drawn interest as heat-responsive biopolymers, such that ELPs undergo reversible phase separation from water upon heating. However, temperature is not always a convenient trigger, especially in biological environments that maintain near-constant temperature, pH, and ionic composition. To expand ELP function, we program a mechanism for isothermal phase separation upon proteolytic cleavage of a di-block ELP. This mechanism presents a new opportunity to exploit biological triggers for ELP phase behavior and self-assembly processes. Overall, we demonstrate repetitive proteins as tunable and modular building blocks for functional biomaterials.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Tesca Fitzgerald Affiliation Yale University Details Event Description Abstract: As our expectations for robots' adaptive capacities grow, it will be increasingly important for them to reason about the novel objects, tasks, and interactions inherent to everyday life. Recent advances in foundation models have produced impressive general-purpose models for robots, but they still need extensive fine-tuning to behave reasonably in novel environments. I argue that we can develop more capable and robust robots by assuming they will inevitably encounter situations that they are initially unprepared to address. My work enables a robot to address these novel situations by learning from a human teacher’s domain knowledge of the task, such as the contextual use of an object or tool. Meeting this challenge requires robots to be flexible not only to novelty, but to different forms of novelty and their varying effects on the robot’s task completion. In this talk, I will focus on (1) the implications of novelty, and its various causes, on the robot’s learning goals, (2) methods for structuring its interaction with the human teacher in order to meet those learning goals, and (3) modeling and learning from interaction-derived training data to address novelty. Abstract: Engineers rely upon models every day in a variety of contexts, up to an including the digital twins that are emerging as an increasingly essential tool for designing, maintaining, and monitoring infrastructure. Unfortunately, as the aphorism goes, “all models are wrong.” Engineers should not lose hope, though, because models can still become useful when they are informed by measurements and observations. In this context, the importance of properly leveraging experimental data for informed model selection and careful parameter estimation becomes apparent. However, the inherent and ubiquitous presence of structural and parametric uncertainties add significant layers of complexity to these modeling tasks, necessitating the use of uncertainty quantification tools such as Bayesian inference. This presentation will discuss various projects located at this nexus of data, modeling, mechanics, and uncertainty. Applications include using novel response data from distributed fiber optics for modal identification, selecting the most probable nonlinear models for seismic isolation systems, and implementing hierarchical Bayesian approaches for calibrating hysteretic models based on experimental data from full-scale shake table testing. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The reading group will explore the intellectual history of machine learning and artificial intelligence, tracing foundational ideas from early theories of neural computation and the perceptron through symbolic AI, the connectionist revival, deep learning, and contemporary foundation models. Rather than studying these methods only in their modern textbook form, we will return to the original papers, debates, and historical context in which they emerged. Sessions will combine readings of foundational work by researchers such as McCulloch and Pitts, Rosenblatt, Minsky and Papert, Hopfield, Rumelhart, Hinton, and McClelland with occasional watch parties featuring archival documentaries, interviews, and television debates from the early history of AI. The group is intended for participants from across machine learning, cognitive science, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, and related fields. No prior background in the history of AI or connectionism is required; the goal is to understand not only how major ideas in machine learning work, but why they emerged, what problems they were intended to solve, and how earlier debates continue to shape AI research today.
