rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The Knight-Georgetown Institute (KGI), the Yale Tobin Center’s Digital Economy Project, and Princeton University’s Center for Information Technology Policy (CITP) will co-host the Digital Competition Conference 2027 (DCC ‘27), an annual policy and research conference that explores the latest lessons, challenges, and opportunities in competition regulation and enforcement in digital markets. The conference brings together researchers, policymakers, regulators, businesses, litigators, technologists, and civil society experts for evidence-driven dialogue about business practices that pose competition risks or may generate other harms, possible remedies, and areas for future analysis. The rapid diffusion of AI and the emergence of AI agents capable of independently accessing tools, initiating processes, and acting on users’ behalf may fundamentally reshape how information and economic activity are organized online. These developments are raising new questions about market power, entry, innovation, and control across the technology stack. At the same time, the regulatory and enforcement disputes that have defined competition policy in tech in recent years continue to evolve, as the implications of incumbent platform power become increasingly consequential. The DCC ‘27 will examine all of these developments through a broad inquiry into competition in digital markets. Building on the success of DCC ‘26 – which brought together participants from 37 countries – the conference will continue to serve as a forum for rigorous, interdisciplinary discussion on the future of competition in the digital economy across key sectors and jurisdictions. The conference aims to advance a shared understanding of competition in AI and digital markets among researchers, policymakers, regulators, business, litigators, technologists, and civil society experts. Discussion will center on research results and methods, what stakeholders know and still need to learn about competition challenges and remedies, and how to create a virtuous cycle where research more effectively informs policymaking and enforcement while regulation enables more effective research. The conference will feature research talks and policy discussions focused on a range of technology markets – as they have been traditionally offered, and as they are being reshaped by AI – including markets for search, chatbots, and AI assistants; consumer and enterprise software, including browsers, apps, harnesses, and cloud services; advertising; social media; messaging; and connected devices. Call for Submissions We are soliciting expressions of interest in researcher participation, including early-stage or draft research papers, prepublication papers, and recent or accepted publications. The program committee will select and curate research talks and poster presentations from the submissions received. With the authors’ consent, we expect to post accepted submissions on our website prior to the conference. Research talks at the conference will be short and should illuminate competition issues, remedies, or research methods. Selected speakers will be asked to stimulate dialogue about the practical application of research findings to policymaking and enforcement. The conference is open to all disciplines, including economics, computer science, law, public policy, business, and behavioral sciences. Topics in Scope While we expect to emphasize AI-related work at the conference, we welcome submissions broadly related to competition in digital markets, including on the following topics: Effectiveness and impact of existing competition regulation of digital platforms How business practices affect competitors and consumers in digital markets, and how regulatory requirements or enforcement remedies would shift market outcomes The impacts of technology competition regulation and enforcement actions, including changes in firm behavior, market structure, and consumer experiences The effectiveness of and further opportunities for platform data sharing, access, transparency, or experimentation requirements Institutional implementation of and compliance with competition regulation Comparison of policy, regulation, and enforcement across jurisdictions, with associated learnings The role of interoperability, portability, open standards, defaults, and choices Open source, open models, and their interplay with competitive dynamics Competition and sustainable information production, including licensing, attribution, and compensation for content used by AI products Consumer protection issues where they intersect with competition, including personalized pricing, algorithmic misrepresentations, hidden fees, dark/deceptive patterns, and other practices that affect market power, entry, or competitive advantage This list is illustrative rather than exhaustive. We welcome work addressing other emerging questions in digital competition, especially where it can shed light on policy design, enforcement, or effectiveness, or market structure specifically in the information ecosystem. Selection priorities The program committee will evaluate submissions with attention to: Policy relevance, including the extent to which findings or ideas can inform real-world policy, regulation, or enforcement Novelty and contribution to the literature, policy debate, or measurement of digital competition issues Methodological rigor and clarity of research design Cross-jurisdictional comparison or broader applicability across institutional settings, where relevant Fit with the conference’s 2027 emphasis on AI, which will receive additional weight but is not a prerequisite for acceptance Since rigorous empirical research on emerging AI markets remains limited, we also welcome well-developed research designs, early findings, measurement frameworks, and work from adjacent fields, provided that submitters are prepared to discuss how their methods and results could be applied or extended to competition challenges and remedies. Guidance for Early-Stage Work We welcome early-stage work, but submissions should be sufficiently developed to support serious discussion at the conference. Research that is qualitative in nature should include a content-complete draft, even if it is not publication-ready. Research that is quantitative in nature but involves complex data collection or analysis should at least have a fully specified research design and a credible plan for completion before the conference. Vague or high-level research proposals or outlines are unlikely to be accepted. Participation Expectations Because the conference is designed around active discussion, accepted submissions should be represented by an author who is prepared to participate substantively in the conference. For coauthored work, we strongly encourage at least one faculty coauthor or other senior lead author to commit to attending and participating. Submission Information Please submit your paper through the submission link by September 25, 2026 . Travel reimbursement will be available for invited conference speakers. Conference timeline Submissions due: September 25, 2026 Speakers notified: November 9, 2026 Speaker registrations due: November 23, 2026 Final paper submission due: January 15, 2027 Conference: February 9-10, 2027 Program committee Alissa Cooper, Knight-Georgetown Institute Filippo Lancieri, Georgetown University Fiona Scott Morton, Yale University Jonathan Mayer, Princeton University Andrew McLean, University of Edinburgh Leon Musolff, University of Pennsylvania Christian Peukert, University of Lausanne Christo Wilson, Northeastern University Tracy Xu, Knight-Georgetown Institute Previous DCCs DCC 2026 DMA and Beyond Contact Please contact the program committee at [email protected] with questions. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description How is it possible that 1/4 of the Nobel Prizes in Physics since 2006 have been for astrophysics? All 5 of them came from new technologies, and two required space observatories. I’ll review the breakthrough ideas that grew into discoveries, and suggest where future technologies might go.The JWST is working brilliantly, and has found Little Red Dots, the current mystery object. But there’s still no Earth 2.0. The DKIST solar telescope with adaptive optics is working beautifully. The Vera Rubin Telescope is online, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will be launched just before this colloquium to study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, and the 39 m diameter Extremely Large Telescope will be doing science around 2030. Among the new possibilities: the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a workhorse UV-near IR observatory with a coronagraph for exoplanets, and X-ray and far IR observatories from Probe class ($1B) to flagships. New detector and mirror technologies are making both exciting. The NAUTILUS concept will use molded glass lenses up to 8 m in diameter in space to collect light for spectroscopy. We’re also developing hybrid observatories combining telescopes and interferometers on the ground with satellites. The Landolt absolute photometric calibrator beacon will fly in 2029, and the CELESTE mission is a proposed Small Explorer to offer a laser beacon for adaptive optics to the ELT, giving it diffraction-limited image quality at visible wavelengths where the sky is darkest. An orbiting starshade could cast a star shadow on the ELT and enable imaging of another Earth in one minute. The Black Hole Explorer would extend the Event Horizon Telescope with an orbiting antenna could measure the spin of a black hole. If you can imagine it, you can build it.
